subject: Business Models
title: Patent Licensing
description: A fast breakdown of Patent Licensing for builders.

hook.text: Qualcomm earns more from licensing its wireless patents than from selling its own chips.

buildup.text: Every smartphone using 3G, 4G, or 5G pays Qualcomm a royalty—typically 3-5% of the phone's price.

discovery.text: With 140,000+ patents, Qualcomm collects billions annually from competitors who must use its technology.

twist.text: Apple sued Qualcomm for $1 billion, calling the fees excessive. They settled, and Apple still pays.

climax.text: Patent licensing turns R&D into a perpetual revenue stream, even if you never make the product yourself.

punchline.text: Invent the standard, then tax every product that uses it.

quiz.question: How does Qualcomm earn most of its revenue?

details.summary: Patent licensing earns revenue by granting other companies the right to use patented technology in their products. Qualcomm earns over 6 billion annually licensing mobile communications patents. IBM, Microsoft, and pharmaceutical companies all generate billions from patent licensing deals.
details.whyItMatters: Patent portfolios can generate revenue long after the original research investment. For some companies, licensing income exceeds manufacturing profits, creating a business model where innovation itself, rather than products.
takeaways: Companies charge fees for others to use their patented technology
Licensing can generate revenue for the full 20-year patent life
Some companies build entire business models around patent portfolios

faq.question: How does Qualcomm's patent licensing model work?
faq.answer: Qualcomm holds essential patents for cellular communication standards including 3G, 4G, and 5G. Every smartphone manufacturer must license these patents to legally sell devices. Qualcomm charges royalties based on the device selling price, generating billions in high-margin licensing revenue.

faq.question: What is the difference between patent licensing and patent trolling?
faq.answer: Legitimate licensing involves companies that developed technology licensing it to others who want to use it. Patent trolls acquire patents they did not invent, then sue companies for infringement to extract settlements. Trolling adds no innovation value and is widely criticized.
